Part 2 (modB) · Linear Algebra and Geometry · Channels A, B and C · Lesson L15

Linear maps II

When two vector spaces are "the same space with different names" (isomorphisms), and how any linear map f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W is turned into a matrix [f]CB[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[f]CB​ by choosing a basis at the start and one at the end. From here on every calculation on polynomials, matrices or abstract vectors becomes a calculation with matrices: it is the tool you need for changes of basis (L16) and for eigenvalues (L17–L18).

lesson 15 · pp. 74–78

The lesson in 9 points

  • An isomorphism is a bijective linear map (injective and surjective). Its inverse f−1f^{-1}f−1 is still linear.
  • The dimensions already say a lot: if f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W is injective then dim⁡V≤dim⁡W\dim V \le \dim WdimV≤dimW; if it is surjective then dim⁡V≥dim⁡W\dim V \ge \dim WdimV≥dimW; if it is an isomorphism then dim⁡V=dim⁡W\dim V = \dim WdimV=dimW.
  • The converse of the last point also holds: two finite-dimensional spaces are isomorphic if and only if they have the same dimension. Every space of dimension nnn over K\KK is isomorphic to Kn\K^nKn: the isomorphism sends every vector to its coordinates [v]B[v]_{\mathcal B}[v]B​ and depends on the basis chosen.
  • Once a basis B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} of VVV and a basis C={w1,…,wm}\mathcal C = \{w_1, \dots, w_m\}C={w1​,…,wm​} of WWW are fixed, every linear f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W has an associated matrix [f]CB[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[f]CB​, of size m×nm \times nm×n: column jjj contains the coordinates of f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​) with respect to C\mathcal CC.
  • Notation rule: the starting basis goes at the top, the target basis goes at the bottom.
  • For LA:Kn→KmL_A : \K^n \to \K^mLA​:Kn→Km with the standard bases the associated matrix is exactly AAA.
  • The key formula is [f(v)]C=[f]CB⋅[v]B[f(v)]_{\mathcal C} = [f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} \cdot [v]_{\mathcal B}[f(v)]C​=[f]CB​⋅[v]B​: in coordinates, every linear map becomes a matrix-times-vector multiplication.
  • The matrix depends on the bases: the same fff has different matrices in different bases. With the same basis at the start and at the end, the identity always has matrix InI_nIn​.
  • The linear maps V→WV \to WV→W form a vector space, and f↦[f]BAf \mapsto [f]^{\mathcal A}_{\mathcal B}f↦[f]BA​ is an isomorphism with M(m,n,K)M(m, n, \K)M(m,n,K).

§1

Isomorphisms: the same space with different names

p. 74

In lesson L14 you saw what a linear map is, the kernel Ker⁡f\Ker fKerf, the image Im⁡f\Imm fImf and the rank–nullity theorem. Here we ask: when do two different vector spaces behave in exactly the same way?

A writing convention, as in the handouts: the vectors of Kn\K^nKn are columns; in the text, to save space, we often write them as rows, like (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2). In the exam papers you also find the notation t(1,2){}^t(1, 2)t(1,2), that is "the transpose of the row (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2)", which is again the column.

An example to start: polynomials and triples of numbers

Take the space R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] of polynomials of degree at most 2. A polynomial a+bx+cx2a + bx + cx^2a+bx+cx2 is determined by its three coefficients, so we can pair it with the triple (a,b,c)∈R3(a, b, c) \in \R^3(a,b,c)∈R3. Look at what happens to the calculations:

In R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x]In R3\R^3R3
p=1+2x+3x2p = 1 + 2x + 3x^2p=1+2x+3x2(1,2,3)(1, 2, 3)(1,2,3)
q=−1+x2q = -1 + x^2q=−1+x2(−1,0,1)(-1, 0, 1)(−1,0,1)
p+q=2x+4x2p + q = 2x + 4x^2p+q=2x+4x2(1,2,3)+(−1,0,1)=(0,2,4)(1, 2, 3) + (-1, 0, 1) = (0, 2, 4)(1,2,3)+(−1,0,1)=(0,2,4)
2q=−2+2x22q = -2 + 2x^22q=−2+2x22⋅(−1,0,1)=(−2,0,2)2 \cdot (-1, 0, 1) = (-2, 0, 2)2⋅(−1,0,1)=(−2,0,2)

Adding polynomials and then taking the coefficients gives the same result as taking the coefficients and then adding the triples. The same for multiples. Moreover the pairing is one-to-one: each polynomial corresponds to exactly one triple and each triple to exactly one polynomial. From the point of view of linear algebra, R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] and R3\R^3R3 are the same space with different names. The technical name is isomorphic (from Greek: "of the same shape").

The definition

Remember three words about functions (you see them in detail in Discrete Mathematics). A function f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W is:

  • injective if different vectors have different images; for a linear map this is equivalent to Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0} (Proposition 14.11);
  • surjective if every w∈Ww \in Ww∈W is the image of some v∈Vv \in Vv∈V, that is Im⁡f=W\Imm f = WImf=W;
  • bijective if it is both injective and surjective. In this case every w∈Ww \in Ww∈W is the image of one and only one vvv, and you can define the inverse function f−1:W→Vf^{-1} : W \to Vf−1:W→V that goes the other way: f−1(f(v))=vf^{-1}(f(v)) = vf−1(f(v))=v and f(f−1(w))=wf(f^{-1}(w)) = wf(f−1(w))=w.

Definition 15.1 · Isomorphism and isomorphic spaces

A linear map f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W is an isomorphism if it is bijective. (Recall that a function fff is bijective if and only if it is both injective and surjective.)

We say that two vector spaces VVV and WWW over the same field K\KK are isomorphic if there exists an isomorphism f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W.

Piece by piece:

  • "linear map" comes first of all: a function that is bijective but not linear is not an isomorphism of vector spaces.
  • "bijective" is checked in two halves: Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0} (injective) and Im⁡f=W\Imm f = WImf=W (surjective).
  • "over the same field": you compare spaces with the same scalars, for example two real spaces.
  • "isomorphic" is a property of the pair of spaces: it is enough that one isomorphism between them exists, even if many other linear maps between the same spaces are not.

Example · three maps, only one is an isomorphism

(a) f=LA:R2→R2f = L_A : \R^2 \to \R^2f=LA​:R2→R2 with A=(2111)A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}A=(21​11​), that is f(x,y)=(2x+y, x+y)f(x, y) = (2x + y,\ x + y)f(x,y)=(2x+y, x+y). Kernel: 2x+y=02x + y = 02x+y=0 and x+y=0x + y = 0x+y=0; subtracting the two equations what remains is x=0x = 0x=0, and then y=0y = 0y=0. So Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0} and fff is injective. By the rank–nullity theorem dim⁡Im⁡f=2−0=2\dim \Imm f = 2 - 0 = 2dimImf=2−0=2, so Im⁡f=R2\Imm f = \R^2Imf=R2 and fff is surjective. It is an isomorphism.

(b) The derivative D:R2[x]→R2[x]D : \R_2[x] \to \R_2[x]D:R2​[x]→R2​[x], D(p)=p′D(p) = p'D(p)=p′. Since D(5)=0D(5) = 0D(5)=0, the constant polynomial 555 lies in the kernel: Ker⁡D≠{0}\Ker D \neq \{0\}KerD={0}, so DDD is not injective and not an isomorphism. (It is not surjective either: the derivative of a polynomial of degree at most 2 has degree at most 1, so x2∉Im⁡Dx^2 \notin \Imm Dx2∈/ImD.)

(c) g:R2→R3g : \R^2 \to \R^3g:R2→R3, g(x,y)=(x,y,0)g(x, y) = (x, y, 0)g(x,y)=(x,y,0). It is injective (if (x,y,0)=(0,0,0)(x, y, 0) = (0, 0, 0)(x,y,0)=(0,0,0) then x=y=0x = y = 0x=y=0) but not surjective: (0,0,1)(0, 0, 1)(0,0,1) is the image of nothing. It is not an isomorphism.

The inverse of an isomorphism is linear

Proposition 15.2

If a linear function f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W is bijective, the inverse f−1:W→Vf^{-1} : W \to Vf−1:W→V is linear too.

Let us see it on example (a). To find f−1(a,b)f^{-1}(a, b)f−1(a,b) we look for (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) with f(x,y)=(a,b)f(x, y) = (a, b)f(x,y)=(a,b):

{2x+y=ax+y=b⟹x=a−b,y=b−x=−a+2b.\begin{cases} 2x + y = a \\ x + y = b \end{cases} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = a - b, \qquad y = b - x = -a + 2b.{2x+y=ax+y=b​⟹x=a−b,y=b−x=−a+2b.

So f−1(a,b)=(a−b, −a+2b)f^{-1}(a, b) = (a - b,\ -a + 2b)f−1(a,b)=(a−b, −a+2b), which is again linear: it is LA−1L_{A^{-1}}LA−1​ with A−1=(1−1−12)A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}A−1=(1−1​−12​). Check: f(3,1)=(7,4)f(3, 1) = (7, 4)f(3,1)=(7,4) and f−1(7,4)=(7−4, −7+8)=(3,1)f^{-1}(7, 4) = (7 - 4,\ -7 + 8) = (3, 1)f−1(7,4)=(7−4, −7+8)=(3,1).

Proof · of Proposition 15.2 (from Martelli's book, §4.2.5; the handouts do not include it)

Let w,w′∈Ww, w' \in Ww,w′∈W and λ∈K\lambda \in \Kλ∈K. We call v=f−1(w)v = f^{-1}(w)v=f−1(w) and v′=f−1(w′)v' = f^{-1}(w')v′=f−1(w′), that is f(v)=wf(v) = wf(v)=w and f(v′)=w′f(v') = w'f(v′)=w′.

  1. Sum. By the linearity of fff: f(v+v′)=f(v)+f(v′)=w+w′f(v + v') = f(v) + f(v') = w + w'f(v+v′)=f(v)+f(v′)=w+w′. So v+v′v + v'v+v′ is the vector that fff sends to w+w′w + w'w+w′, that is f−1(w+w′)=v+v′=f−1(w)+f−1(w′)f^{-1}(w + w') = v + v' = f^{-1}(w) + f^{-1}(w')f−1(w+w′)=v+v′=f−1(w)+f−1(w′).
  2. Multiples. f(λv)=λf(v)=λwf(\lambda v) = \lambda f(v) = \lambda wf(λv)=λf(v)=λw, so f−1(λw)=λv=λf−1(w)f^{-1}(\lambda w) = \lambda v = \lambda f^{-1}(w)f−1(λw)=λv=λf−1(w).

In each step you use that fff is bijective: the vector that goes to w+w′w + w'w+w′ (or to λw\lambda wλw) is unique, so it is exactly the one found.

What the dimensions say

Proposition 15.3

Let f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W be a linear map.

  1. If fff is injective, then dim⁡V≤dim⁡W\dim V \le \dim WdimV≤dimW. (Indeed dim⁡V=dim⁡Im⁡f≤dim⁡W\dim V = \dim \Imm f \le \dim WdimV=dimImf≤dimW.)
  2. If fff is surjective, then dim⁡V≥dim⁡W\dim V \ge \dim WdimV≥dimW. (Indeed dim⁡V≥dim⁡Im⁡f=dim⁡W\dim V \ge \dim \Imm f = \dim WdimV≥dimImf=dimW.)
  3. If fff is an isomorphism, then dim⁡V=dim⁡W\dim V = \dim WdimV=dimW. (From the two previous points.)

The justifications in brackets use the rank–nullity theorem of lesson L14, dim⁡V=dim⁡Ker⁡f+dim⁡Im⁡f\dim V = \dim \Ker f + \dim \Imm fdimV=dimKerf+dimImf:

  1. if fff is injective, Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0}, so dim⁡V=0+dim⁡Im⁡f\dim V = 0 + \dim \Imm fdimV=0+dimImf; and Im⁡f\Imm fImf is a subspace of WWW, so dim⁡Im⁡f≤dim⁡W\dim \Imm f \le \dim WdimImf≤dimW;
  2. if fff is surjective, Im⁡f=W\Imm f = WImf=W, so dim⁡V=dim⁡Ker⁡f+dim⁡W≥dim⁡W\dim V = \dim \Ker f + \dim W \ge \dim WdimV=dimKerf+dimW≥dimW;
  3. an isomorphism is both injective and surjective, so both inequalities hold.

In practice, looking only at the dimensions you can rule out many things:

DimensionsCan it be injective?Can it be surjective?Can it be an isomorphism?
dim⁡V<dim⁡W\dim V < \dim WdimV<dimW (for example R2→R3\R^2 \to \R^3R2→R3)yesnevernever
dim⁡V>dim⁡W\dim V > \dim WdimV>dimW (for example R4→R2\R^4 \to \R^2R4→R2)neveryesnever
dim⁡V=dim⁡W\dim V = \dim WdimV=dimWyesyesyes

Pitfall · The dimensions rule out, they do not guarantee

dim⁡V≤dim⁡W\dim V \le \dim WdimV≤dimW is not enough to say that fff is injective: the zero map R2→R3\R^2 \to \R^3R2→R3, f(v)=0f(v) = 0f(v)=0, has dim⁡V=2≤3\dim V = 2 \le 3dimV=2≤3 but kernel equal to the whole of R2\R^2R2. Proposition 15.3 only says what happens if fff is injective (or surjective). To prove that a specific fff is injective you have to compute the kernel.

Same dimension, isomorphic spaces

The converse of the last point also holds:

Proposition 15.4

Let VVV and WWW be two finite-dimensional vector spaces. Then

V and W are isomorphic  ⟺  dim⁡V=dim⁡W.V \text{ and } W \text{ are isomorphic} \iff \dim V = \dim W.V and W are isomorphic⟺dimV=dimW.

In particular, all the vector spaces over K\KK of dimension nnn are isomorphic to Kn\K^nKn.

The handouts specify which isomorphism to use: the map V→KnV \to \K^nV→Kn that sends every vector v∈Vv \in Vv∈V to its coordinates with respect to a basis of VVV (you saw them in lesson L13, Definition 13.5). This isomorphism depends on the choice of the basis.

Example · the same polynomial, two different coordinate vectors

In R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] take the standard basis B={1,x,x2}\mathcal B = \{1, x, x^2\}B={1,x,x2} and the basis B′={1, x−1, (x−1)2}\mathcal B' = \{1,\ x - 1,\ (x - 1)^2\}B′={1, x−1, (x−1)2}. The polynomial x2x^2x2 has coordinates (0,0,1)(0, 0, 1)(0,0,1) with respect to B\mathcal BB. With respect to B′\mathcal B'B′ we look for a,b,ca, b, ca,b,c with

x2=a⋅1+b (x−1)+c (x−1)2=(a−b+c)+(b−2c) x+c x2.x^2 = a \cdot 1 + b\,(x - 1) + c\,(x - 1)^2 = (a - b + c) + (b - 2c)\,x + c\,x^2.x2=a⋅1+b(x−1)+c(x−1)2=(a−b+c)+(b−2c)x+cx2.

Comparing the coefficients: c=1c = 1c=1, then b−2c=0b - 2c = 0b−2c=0 gives b=2b = 2b=2, then a−b+c=0a - b + c = 0a−b+c=0 gives a=1a = 1a=1. So the coordinates are (1,2,1)(1, 2, 1)(1,2,1). Check: 1+2(x−1)+(x−1)2=1+2x−2+x2−2x+1=x21 + 2(x - 1) + (x - 1)^2 = 1 + 2x - 2 + x^2 - 2x + 1 = x^21+2(x−1)+(x−1)2=1+2x−2+x2−2x+1=x2.

The two bases give two different isomorphisms R2[x]→R3\R_2[x] \to \R^3R2​[x]→R3: the first sends x2x^2x2 to (0,0,1)(0, 0, 1)(0,0,1), the second to (1,2,1)(1, 2, 1)(1,2,1).

Beyond the handouts · how the isomorphism is built, and a useful shortcut

Why ⇐\Leftarrow⇐ holds (Martelli, Proposition 4.2.30). If dim⁡V=dim⁡W=n\dim V = \dim W = ndimV=dimW=n, choose a basis v1,…,vnv_1, \dots, v_nv1​,…,vn​ of VVV and a basis w1,…,wnw_1, \dots, w_nw1​,…,wn​ of WWW, and define fff by imposing f(vi)=wif(v_i) = w_if(vi​)=wi​ and extending by linearity, f(λ1v1+⋯+λnvn)=λ1w1+⋯+λnwnf(\lambda_1 v_1 + \dots + \lambda_n v_n) = \lambda_1 w_1 + \dots + \lambda_n w_nf(λ1​v1​+⋯+λn​vn​)=λ1​w1​+⋯+λn​wn​ (Martelli, Proposition 4.1.18). The image contains all the wiw_iwi​, so Im⁡f=W\Imm f = WImf=W; by the rank–nullity theorem dim⁡Ker⁡f=n−n=0\dim \Ker f = n - n = 0dimKerf=n−n=0. So fff is bijective.

The shortcut (Martelli, Proposition 4.2.24). If dim⁡V=dim⁡W\dim V = \dim WdimV=dimW, for a linear map f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W the three things "injective", "surjective", "isomorphism" are equivalent: it is enough to check one. Indeed dim⁡Ker⁡f=0  ⟺  dim⁡Im⁡f=n  ⟺  Im⁡f=W\dim \Ker f = 0 \iff \dim \Imm f = n \iff \Imm f = WdimKerf=0⟺dimImf=n⟺Imf=W. For a square matrix AAA this is summed up as: LAL_ALA​ is an isomorphism   ⟺  det⁡A≠0  ⟺  rk⁡A=n\iff \det A \neq 0 \iff \rk A = n⟺detA=0⟺rkA=n.

§2

Coordinates of a vector

p. 74

The whole rest of the lesson uses coordinates, so let us go over them calmly. If B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} is a basis of VVV, every v∈Vv \in Vv∈V can be written in only one way (Proposition 13.4) as

v=λ1v1+⋯+λnvn.v = \lambda_1 v_1 + \dots + \lambda_n v_n.v=λ1​v1​+⋯+λn​vn​.

The column of coefficients is called the coordinate vector of vvv with respect to B\mathcal BB and is written

[v]B=(λ1⋮λn)∈Kn.[v]_{\mathcal B} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 \\ \vdots \\ \lambda_n \end{pmatrix} \in \K^n.[v]B​=​λ1​⋮λn​​​∈Kn.

Example · coordinates in a non-standard basis of R2\R^2R2

Let B={v1,v2}\mathcal B = \{v_1, v_2\}B={v1​,v2​} with v1=(1,1)v_1 = (1, 1)v1​=(1,1) and v2=(1,−1)v_2 = (1, -1)v2​=(1,−1), and let v=(3,1)v = (3, 1)v=(3,1). We look for λ1,λ2\lambda_1, \lambda_2λ1​,λ2​ with λ1(1,1)+λ2(1,−1)=(3,1)\lambda_1 (1, 1) + \lambda_2 (1, -1) = (3, 1)λ1​(1,1)+λ2​(1,−1)=(3,1):

{λ1+λ2=3λ1−λ2=1\begin{cases} \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 3 \\ \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 1 \end{cases}{λ1​+λ2​=3λ1​−λ2​=1​

Adding the equations: 2λ1=42\lambda_1 = 42λ1​=4, that is λ1=2\lambda_1 = 2λ1​=2; then λ2=3−2=1\lambda_2 = 3 - 2 = 1λ2​=3−2=1. So [v]B=(2,1)[v]_{\mathcal B} = (2, 1)[v]B​=(2,1): to reach vvv you take two steps along v1v_1v1​ and one along v2v_2v2​.

Pitfall · The order of the basis vectors matters

For coordinates, a basis is an ordered list. With B′={v2,v1}\mathcal B' = \{v_2, v_1\}B′={v2​,v1​} (same vectors, order swapped) the same vvv has coordinates (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2). That is why, even though it is written with curly brackets, B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} must be read as a list in that order.

§3

The matrix associated with a linear map

pp. 74–75

The idea

In lesson L14 you saw that a linear map respects linear combinations:

f(λ1v1+⋯+λnvn)=λ1f(v1)+⋯+λnf(vn).f(\lambda_1 v_1 + \dots + \lambda_n v_n) = \lambda_1 f(v_1) + \dots + \lambda_n f(v_n).f(λ1​v1​+⋯+λn​vn​)=λ1​f(v1​)+⋯+λn​f(vn​).

So, if you know the images of the vectors of a basis, f(v1),…,f(vn)f(v_1), \dots, f(v_n)f(v1​),…,f(vn​), you know fff everywhere. Each f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​) is a vector of WWW: we store it with its mmm coordinates with respect to a basis C\mathcal CC of WWW. We get nnn columns of mmm numbers: an m×nm \times nm×n matrix. This is the associated matrix.

Definition 15.5 · Associated matrix

Let f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W be a linear map between vector spaces defined over K\KK. Let moreover

B={v1,…,vn},C={w1,…,wm}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}, \qquad \mathcal C = \{w_1, \dots, w_m\}B={v1​,…,vn​},C={w1​,…,wm​}

be two bases of VVV and of WWW respectively. We know that

f(v1)=a11w1+⋯+am1wm,  ⋮f(vn)=a1nw1+⋯+amnwm\begin{aligned} f(v_1) &= a_{11} w_1 + \dots + a_{m1} w_m, \\ &\ \ \vdots \\ f(v_n) &= a_{1n} w_1 + \dots + a_{mn} w_m \end{aligned}f(v1​)f(vn​)​=a11​w1​+⋯+am1​wm​,  ⋮=a1n​w1​+⋯+amn​wm​​

for some set of coefficients aij∈Ka_{ij} \in \Kaij​∈K. We define the matrix associated with fff in the bases B\mathcal BB and C\mathcal CC as the m×nm \times nm×n matrix

A=(aij)A = (a_{ij})A=(aij​)

that collects these coefficients, and we denote it by the symbol A=[f]CBA = [f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}A=[f]CB​.

Piece by piece:

  • Size m×nm \times nm×n: as many rows as the dimension of the target space (m=dim⁡Wm = \dim Wm=dimW), as many columns as the dimension of the starting space (n=dim⁡Vn = \dim Vn=dimV).
  • The entry aija_{ij}aij​ is the iii-th coordinate of f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​): the index jjj says which vector of the starting basis you are transforming, the index iii says which coordinate of the image you are reading.
  • The notation [f]CB[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[f]CB​ reminds you that the matrix depends on three things: fff, B\mathcal BB and C\mathcal CC. As the handouts say, "the starting basis" B\mathcal BB goes at the top, "the target basis" C\mathcal CC goes at the bottom.
  • Column jjj, which the handouts call AjA^jAj, contains the coordinates of f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​) with respect to C\mathcal CC:
    Aj=(a1j⋮amj)=[f(vj)]C.A^j = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1j} \\ \vdots \\ a_{mj} \end{pmatrix} = [f(v_j)]_{\mathcal C}.Aj=​a1j​⋮amj​​​=[f(vj​)]C​.

Pitfall · The coefficients go in a column, not in a row

In the definition the first equation, f(v1)=a11w1+⋯+am1wmf(v_1) = a_{11} w_1 + \dots + a_{m1} w_mf(v1​)=a11​w1​+⋯+am1​wm​, fills the first column. If you write the coordinates of f(v1)f(v_1)f(v1​) in the first row you get the transpose, which is wrong. In the exam papers the transpose almost always appears among the wrong answers.

Method · The associated matrix in three steps

  1. Compute the images f(v1),…,f(vn)f(v_1), \dots, f(v_n)f(v1​),…,f(vn​) of the vectors of the starting basis, in the given order.
  2. Write each f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​) in coordinates with respect to the target basis C\mathcal CC. If C\mathcal CC is the standard basis of Km\K^mKm the coordinates are the components themselves; otherwise solve the system f(vj)=x1w1+⋯+xmwmf(v_j) = x_1 w_1 + \dots + x_m w_mf(vj​)=x1​w1​+⋯+xm​wm​.
  3. Put [f(vj)]C[f(v_j)]_{\mathcal C}[f(vj​)]C​ in column jjj.

Quick check: the matrix must have dim⁡W\dim WdimW rows and dim⁡V\dim VdimV columns.

The case of the standard bases

Example 15.6 · The matrix of LAL_ALA​

The matrix associated with LAL_ALA​ with respect to the standard bases of Kn\K^nKn and Km\K^mKm is exactly AAA. Indeed, by construction, f(ej)=a1je1+⋯+amjemf(e_j) = a_{1j} e_1 + \dots + a_{mj} e_mf(ej​)=a1j​e1​+⋯+amj​em​.

With numbers: let A=(120013)A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}A=(10​21​03​), so LA:R3→R2L_A : \R^3 \to \R^2LA​:R3→R2. Then LA(e1)=Ae1L_A(e_1) = A e_1LA​(e1​)=Ae1​ is the first column of AAA, that is (1,0)=1⋅e1+0⋅e2(1, 0) = 1 \cdot e_1 + 0 \cdot e_2(1,0)=1⋅e1​+0⋅e2​; its coordinates with respect to the standard basis are (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0), and they end up in the first column. The same for e2e_2e2​ and e3e_3e3​: you find AAA again. That is why, with the standard bases, the associated matrix of f(x,y,z)=(x+2y, y+3z)f(x, y, z) = (x + 2y,\ y + 3z)f(x,y,z)=(x+2y, y+3z) is read off the coefficients: first row 1,2,01, 2, 01,2,0, second row 0,1,30, 1, 30,1,3.

An example with polynomials

Example 15.7 · Values of a polynomial at 222 and at −2-2−2

Consider the linear map

f:R2[x]⟶R2,f(p)=(p(2)p(−2))f : \R_2[x] \longrightarrow \R^2, \qquad f(p) = \begin{pmatrix} p(2) \\ p(-2) \end{pmatrix}f:R2​[x]⟶R2,f(p)=(p(2)p(−2)​)

which assigns to every polynomial its values at 222 and at −2-2−2. We write the matrix associated with fff in the standard bases B={1,x,x2}\mathcal B = \{1, x, x^2\}B={1,x,x2} of R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] and C={e1,e2}\mathcal C = \{e_1, e_2\}C={e1​,e2​} of R2\R^2R2.

Step 1, the images of the starting basis:

  • p=1p = 1p=1 (the constant polynomial): p(2)=1p(2) = 1p(2)=1 and p(−2)=1p(-2) = 1p(−2)=1, so f(1)=(1,1)f(1) = (1, 1)f(1)=(1,1);
  • p=xp = xp=x: p(2)=2p(2) = 2p(2)=2 and p(−2)=−2p(-2) = -2p(−2)=−2, so f(x)=(2,−2)f(x) = (2, -2)f(x)=(2,−2);
  • p=x2p = x^2p=x2: p(2)=4p(2) = 4p(2)=4 and p(−2)=(−2)2=4p(-2) = (-2)^2 = 4p(−2)=(−2)2=4, so f(x2)=(4,4)f(x^2) = (4, 4)f(x2)=(4,4).

Step 2: the target basis is the standard one, so the coordinates are the components themselves.

Step 3, the three columns side by side:

[f]CB=(1241−24).[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.[f]CB​=(11​2−2​44​).

It is 2×32 \times 32×3: dim⁡R2=2\dim \R^2 = 2dimR2=2 rows, dim⁡R2[x]=3\dim \R_2[x] = 3dimR2​[x]=3 columns.

Same map, another target basis

Example 15.8 · We change the target basis

We take the linear map fff and the basis B\mathcal BB as in the previous example, but at the end we take the basis

C′={(1−1),(01)}\mathcal C' = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}C′={(1−1​),(01​)}

instead of the standard basis C\mathcal CC. The images are the same as before; step 2 changes: you must compute the coordinates of each image with respect to C′\mathcal C'C′, that is find a,ba, ba,b with a(1,−1)+b(0,1)=(a, −a+b)a (1, -1) + b (0, 1) = (a,\ -a + b)a(1,−1)+b(0,1)=(a, −a+b) equal to the image.

  • f(1)=(1,1)f(1) = (1, 1)f(1)=(1,1): first component a=1a = 1a=1; second −1+b=1-1 + b = 1−1+b=1, so b=2b = 2b=2. So (1,1)=1⋅(1,−1)+2⋅(0,1)(1, 1) = 1 \cdot (1, -1) + 2 \cdot (0, 1)(1,1)=1⋅(1,−1)+2⋅(0,1).
  • f(x)=(2,−2)f(x) = (2, -2)f(x)=(2,−2): a=2a = 2a=2; −2+b=−2-2 + b = -2−2+b=−2, so b=0b = 0b=0. So (2,−2)=2⋅(1,−1)+0⋅(0,1)(2, -2) = 2 \cdot (1, -1) + 0 \cdot (0, 1)(2,−2)=2⋅(1,−1)+0⋅(0,1).
  • f(x2)=(4,4)f(x^2) = (4, 4)f(x2)=(4,4): a=4a = 4a=4; −4+b=4-4 + b = 4−4+b=4, so b=8b = 8b=8. So (4,4)=4⋅(1,−1)+8⋅(0,1)(4, 4) = 4 \cdot (1, -1) + 8 \cdot (0, 1)(4,4)=4⋅(1,−1)+8⋅(0,1).

The associated matrix therefore becomes

[f]C′B=(124208).[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C'} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix}.[f]C′B​=(12​20​48​).

The same fff has two different matrices: the associated matrix depends on the bases. In lesson L16 you will see the formula that goes from one to the other with a product of matrices. In exercise 6 you find a third target basis that makes the matrix simpler.

To solve the systems of step 2 you can use the tool below. It is already set up with the system of exercise 15.13 (exercise 1): the first three columns are the vectors w1=(1,1,0)w_1 = (1, 1, 0)w1​=(1,1,0), w2=(0,1,1)w_2 = (0, 1, 1)w2​=(0,1,1), w3=(1,0,1)w_3 = (1, 0, 1)w3​=(1,0,1) of the target basis, the last is the vector f(v1)=(0,2,1)f(v_1) = (0, 2, 1)f(v1​)=(0,2,1) whose coordinates you are looking for. The solution (x1,x2,x3)(x_1, x_2, x_3)(x1​,x2​,x3​) is the column [f(v1)]C[f(v_1)]_{\mathcal C}[f(v1​)]C​. Then try changing the last column to (2,2,−1)(2, 2, -1)(2,2,−1) to get the second column of the matrix.

§4

Computing images with the matrix

pp. 76–77

From the associated matrix we can compute the image of any vector. Let f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W be a linear map and let B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} and C={w1,…,wm}\mathcal C = \{w_1, \dots, w_m\}C={w1​,…,wm​} be bases of VVV and WWW.

Proposition 15.9

For every v∈Vv \in Vv∈V we find

[f(v)]C=[f]CB⋅[v]B.[f(v)]_{\mathcal C} = [f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} \cdot [v]_{\mathcal B}.[f(v)]C​=[f]CB​⋅[v]B​.

In words: to find the coordinates of f(v)f(v)f(v) with respect to C\mathcal CC it is enough to multiply the associated matrix by the coordinates of vvv with respect to B\mathcal BB. The handouts' proof, with the steps explained:

  1. We write vvv in the basis B\mathcal BB: v=λ1v1+⋯+λnvnv = \lambda_1 v_1 + \dots + \lambda_n v_nv=λ1​v1​+⋯+λn​vn​, so [v]B=(λ1,…,λn)[v]_{\mathcal B} = (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)[v]B​=(λ1​,…,λn​).
  2. By the linearity of fff: f(v)=λ1f(v1)+⋯+λnf(vn)f(v) = \lambda_1 f(v_1) + \dots + \lambda_n f(v_n)f(v)=λ1​f(v1​)+⋯+λn​f(vn​).
  3. Taking coordinates is linear too (it is the isomorphism of Proposition 15.4), so
    [f(v)]C=λ1[f(v1)]C+⋯+λn[f(vn)]C.[f(v)]_{\mathcal C} = \lambda_1 [f(v_1)]_{\mathcal C} + \dots + \lambda_n [f(v_n)]_{\mathcal C}.[f(v)]C​=λ1​[f(v1​)]C​+⋯+λn​[f(vn​)]C​.
  4. But [f(vj)]C[f(v_j)]_{\mathcal C}[f(vj​)]C​ is column jjj of the associated matrix A=(aij)A = (a_{ij})A=(aij​). And a combination of the columns with coefficients λ1,…,λn\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ is exactly the row-by-column product A⋅(λ1,…,λn)A \cdot (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)A⋅(λ1​,…,λn​): component iii of the combination is ai1λ1+⋯+ainλna_{i1}\lambda_1 + \dots + a_{in}\lambda_nai1​λ1​+⋯+ain​λn​, that is exactly row iii of the product. So the result is [f]CB⋅[v]B[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} \cdot [v]_{\mathcal B}[f]CB​⋅[v]B​. □\square□

Remark · Every linear map, in coordinates, is an LAL_ALA​

If we write x=[v]Bx = [v]_{\mathcal B}x=[v]B​, A=[f]CBA = [f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}A=[f]CB​ and y=[f(v)]Cy = [f(v)]_{\mathcal C}y=[f(v)]C​, then

y=Ax=LA(x).y = Ax = L_A(x).y=Ax=LA​(x).

This means that, after choosing two bases for VVV and WWW, any linear map V→WV \to WV→W can be interpreted in coordinates as a map of the form LA:Kn→KmL_A : \K^n \to \K^mLA​:Kn→Km. It is enough to replace the vectors vvv and f(v)f(v)f(v) with their coordinates xxx and yyy, and use the associated matrix AAA.

The diagram below sums up the remark: you get from vvv to the coordinates of f(v)f(v)f(v) by two routes, and the result is the same. At the top you work with the real vectors (polynomials, matrices, …), at the bottom only with columns of numbers.

Example 15.10 · The image of a polynomial computed with the matrix

We take again the associated matrix with respect to the standard bases

[f]CB=(1241−24).[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.[f]CB​=(11​2−2​44​).

We use it to compute in coordinates the image of p(x)=3x2+5x+1p(x) = 3x^2 + 5x + 1p(x)=3x2+5x+1, which has as coordinates with respect to B={1,x,x2}\mathcal B = \{1, x, x^2\}B={1,x,x2} its coefficients in reverse order: [p]B=(1,5,3)[p]_{\mathcal B} = (1, 5, 3)[p]B​=(1,5,3). So f(p)f(p)f(p) has coordinates

(1241−24)(153)=(1⋅1+2⋅5+4⋅31⋅1−2⋅5+4⋅3)=(1+10+121−10+12)=(233).\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 5 + 4 \cdot 3 \\ 1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 5 + 4 \cdot 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 10 + 12 \\ 1 - 10 + 12 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 23 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}.(11​2−2​44​)​153​​=(1⋅1+2⋅5+4⋅31⋅1−2⋅5+4⋅3​)=(1+10+121−10+12​)=(233​).

We check with the definition of fff: p(2)=3⋅4+5⋅2+1=23p(2) = 3 \cdot 4 + 5 \cdot 2 + 1 = 23p(2)=3⋅4+5⋅2+1=23 and p(−2)=3⋅4−10+1=3p(-2) = 3 \cdot 4 - 10 + 1 = 3p(−2)=3⋅4−10+1=3. So f(p)=(23,3)f(p) = (23, 3)f(p)=(23,3).

Note · A cross-reference to correct

In the handouts, on p. 77, Example 15.10 starts with "In Example 15.8 above, we obtained the associated matrix … with respect to the standard bases". The matrix with respect to the standard bases, (1241−24)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}(11​2−2​44​), is the one of Example 15.7; Example 15.8 uses the basis C′\mathcal C'C′ at the end.

Example · the same calculation with the basis C′\mathcal C'C′

With the matrix of Example 15.8:

[f(p)]C′=(124208)(153)=(1+10+122+0+24)=(2326).[f(p)]_{\mathcal C'} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 10 + 12 \\ 2 + 0 + 24 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 23 \\ 26 \end{pmatrix}.[f(p)]C′​=(12​20​48​)​153​​=(1+10+122+0+24​)=(2326​).

Careful: (23,26)(23, 26)(23,26) is not f(p)f(p)f(p), they are its coordinates with respect to C′\mathcal C'C′. To go back to the vector you take the combination: 23⋅(1,−1)+26⋅(0,1)=(23, −23+26)=(23,3)23 \cdot (1, -1) + 26 \cdot (0, 1) = (23,\ -23 + 26) = (23, 3)23⋅(1,−1)+26⋅(0,1)=(23, −23+26)=(23,3). Same result as before, as it must be.

Pitfall · Coordinates or vector?

The product [f]CB⋅[v]B[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} \cdot [v]_{\mathcal B}[f]CB​⋅[v]B​ gives the coordinates of f(v)f(v)f(v) with respect to C\mathcal CC. They coincide with f(v)f(v)f(v) only if C\mathcal CC is the standard basis of Km\K^mKm. And before multiplying you must put vvv in coordinates with respect to B\mathcal BB: for a polynomial, the coefficients in the order of the basis (for {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2}: constant term, then xxx, then x2x^2x2).

§5

The matrix of the identity

p. 77

A special case, useful in the future:

Proposition 15.11

Let B\mathcal BB be any basis of a space VVV of dimension nnn. We find

[id⁡]BB=In.[\id]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal B} = I_n.[id]BB​=In​.

The reason: id⁡(vj)=vj=0⋅v1+⋯+1⋅vj+⋯+0⋅vn\id(v_j) = v_j = 0 \cdot v_1 + \dots + 1 \cdot v_j + \dots + 0 \cdot v_nid(vj​)=vj​=0⋅v1​+⋯+1⋅vj​+⋯+0⋅vn​, so column jjj is the vector eje_jej​, with a 1 in place jjj and zeros elsewhere. All the columns together form the identity matrix.

Pitfall · With two different bases the identity does not have matrix InI_nIn​

Proposition 15.11 requires the same basis at the start and at the end. With B={(1,1),(1,−1)}\mathcal B = \{(1, 1), (1, -1)\}B={(1,1),(1,−1)} at the start and the standard basis C\mathcal CC at the end, the columns are [id⁡(v1)]C=(1,1)[\id(v_1)]_{\mathcal C} = (1, 1)[id(v1​)]C​=(1,1) and [id⁡(v2)]C=(1,−1)[\id(v_2)]_{\mathcal C} = (1, -1)[id(v2​)]C​=(1,−1):

[id⁡]CB=(111−1)≠I2.[\id]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \neq I_2.[id]CB​=(11​1−1​)=I2​.

This is a change-of-basis matrix, the topic of lesson L16.

§6

The space of linear maps

pp. 77–78

Linear maps can be added and multiplied by a scalar, "point by point". If V,WV, WV,W are vector spaces and f,g:V→Wf, g : V \to Wf,g:V→W two linear maps, for λ∈K\lambda \in \Kλ∈K one defines

(f+g)(v)=f(v)+g(v),(λf)(v)=λf(v).(f + g)(v) = f(v) + g(v), \qquad (\lambda f)(v) = \lambda f(v).(f+g)(v)=f(v)+g(v),(λf)(v)=λf(v).

With these two operations the set of all the linear maps between VVV and WWW becomes a vector space: the zero is the zero map, and the properties of sum and product are inherited from those of WWW.

Example · adding maps = adding matrices

Let f,g:R2→R2f, g : \R^2 \to \R^2f,g:R2→R2 with f(x,y)=(x+y, 0)f(x, y) = (x + y,\ 0)f(x,y)=(x+y, 0) and g(x,y)=(x, y)g(x, y) = (x,\ y)g(x,y)=(x, y). Then

(f+g)(x,y)=(x+y+x, 0+y)=(2x+y, y),(3f)(x,y)=(3x+3y, 0).(f + g)(x, y) = (x + y + x,\ 0 + y) = (2x + y,\ y), \qquad (3f)(x, y) = (3x + 3y,\ 0).(f+g)(x,y)=(x+y+x, 0+y)=(2x+y, y),(3f)(x,y)=(3x+3y, 0).

With the standard bases: [f]=(1100)[f] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}[f]=(10​10​), [g]=(1001)[g] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}[g]=(10​01​) and

[f+g]=(2101)=[f]+[g],[3f]=(3300)=3 [f].[f + g] = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = [f] + [g], \qquad [3f] = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = 3\,[f].[f+g]=(20​11​)=[f]+[g],[3f]=(30​30​)=3[f].

Theorem 15.12

Let V,WV, WV,W be two finite-dimensional vector spaces with bases A={v1,…,vn}\mathcal A = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}A={v1​,…,vn​}, B={w1,…,wm}\mathcal B = \{w_1, \dots, w_m\}B={w1​,…,wm​}, respectively. Then the set of linear maps f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W is a vector space, and the map

f⟼[f]BAf \longmapsto [f]^{\mathcal A}_{\mathcal B}f⟼[f]BA​

from the set of linear maps f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W to M(m,n,K)M(m, n, \K)M(m,n,K) is an isomorphism.

Piece by piece (careful: here the bases are called A\mathcal AA and B\mathcal BB, with B\mathcal BB a basis of WWW):

  • It is linear: column jjj of [f+g][f + g][f+g] is [f(vj)+g(vj)]B=[f(vj)]B+[g(vj)]B[f(v_j) + g(v_j)]_{\mathcal B} = [f(v_j)]_{\mathcal B} + [g(v_j)]_{\mathcal B}[f(vj​)+g(vj​)]B​=[f(vj​)]B​+[g(vj​)]B​, so [f+g]=[f]+[g][f + g] = [f] + [g][f+g]=[f]+[g]; in the same way [λf]=λ[f][\lambda f] = \lambda [f][λf]=λ[f]. It is what you saw in the example.
  • It is injective: if [f]=0[f] = 0[f]=0, all the images f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​) are zero, and then fff is the zero map.
  • It is surjective: every matrix A=(aij)A = (a_{ij})A=(aij​) is the matrix of some fff. It is enough to define fff on the basis, f(vj)=a1jw1+⋯+amjwmf(v_j) = a_{1j} w_1 + \dots + a_{mj} w_mf(vj​)=a1j​w1​+⋯+amj​wm​, and extend by linearity.

In practice: once the bases are chosen, linear maps and matrices are the same thing. Everything that is proved for matrices holds for linear maps, and vice versa.

Beyond the handouts · Hom and its dimension

In Martelli's book (§4.3.4) the set of linear maps V→WV \to WV→W is called Hom(V,W)\mathrm{Hom}(V, W)Hom(V,W), from "homomorphism", a synonym of linear map. Since it is isomorphic to M(m,n,K)M(m, n, \K)M(m,n,K), it has dimension mnmnmn (Corollary 4.3.12). For example the linear maps R3→R2\R^3 \to \R^2R3→R2 form a space of dimension 2⋅3=62 \cdot 3 = 62⋅3=6.

One way to see the associated matrix in action is the tool below: a 2×22 \times 22×2 matrix as a transformation of the plane. With A=(2111)A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}A=(21​11​), the isomorphism of example (a), the columns are the images of e1e_1e1​ and e2e_2e2​ and the unit square becomes a parallelogram of area ∣det⁡A∣=1|\det A| = 1∣detA∣=1. Then try typing A=(1224)A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}A=(12​24​): the plane gets squashed onto a line, the kernel is no longer {0}\{0\}{0} and LAL_ALA​ is not an isomorphism.

Beyond the handouts · where to find it in the book

In Martelli's book: §4.2.5 "Isomorfismi" (pp. 127–128, with the proof of Proposition 15.2 and the shortcut of Proposition 4.2.24), §4.2.7 "Spazi vettoriali isomorfi" (p. 129), §4.3 "Matrice associata" up to §4.3.4 "Hom" (pp. 130–135). Examples 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 of the book are Examples 15.7–15.8 and Exercise 15.13 of the handouts.

§7

Towards the exam

exam

The Linear Algebra and Geometry test has 10 multiple-choice questions (5 answers, one right) and 2 problems worth 11 points, which are marked only with at least 6 correct answers; it lasts 2 hours, with no calculator, and you may bring only a 4-page handwritten sheet. The 2026/27 exam sessions are on 22/01 and 05/02/2027 at 14:00. All the details are in lesson L01.

What you need from this lesson for the exam

  1. The associated matrix is one of the most frequent quiz questions. In the 2023–2026 exam papers it appears like this: matrix of T:R2→R2T : \R^2 \to \R^2T:R2→R2 with respect to a non-standard basis (exam of 24/01/2024, question 3, and of 15/01/2026, question 8); coordinates [T(v1)]B[T(v_1)]_{\mathcal B}[T(v1​)]B​ of an image (05/02/2026, question 6); matrix of a composition (16/01/2025, question 5, which you will see in lesson L16). Tutoring sheet 3 (exercises 4 and 5) trains exactly this.
  2. The dimension arguments of Proposition 15.3 give the answer in one line: exam of 02/09/2025, question 5.
  3. In the open problems you are often asked to write the matrix of TTT in the standard basis and to say whether TTT is bijective (exam of 10/07/2024, problem 11), or to compute kernel and image starting from the matrix.
  4. The whole part on eigenvalues (lessons L17–L18) uses the associated matrix: for an endomorphism of R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] you work with its 3×33 \times 33×3 matrix.

Three real exam questions, solved

Matters in the exam · Exam of 15/01/2026, question 8

The matrix associated with T:R2→R2T : \R^2 \to \R^2T:R2→R2, T(x,y)=(2x,3y)T(x, y) = (2x, 3y)T(x,y)=(2x,3y), with respect to the basis B={(0,1),(1,2)}\mathcal B = \{(0, 1), (1, 2)\}B={(0,1),(1,2)} is … (meaning [T]BB[T]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal B}[T]BB​, the same basis at the start and at the end).

Solution. Step 1: T(0,1)=(0,3)T(0, 1) = (0, 3)T(0,1)=(0,3) and T(1,2)=(2,6)T(1, 2) = (2, 6)T(1,2)=(2,6). Step 2, coordinates with respect to B\mathcal BB: a(0,1)+b(1,2)=(b, a+2b)a (0, 1) + b (1, 2) = (b,\ a + 2b)a(0,1)+b(1,2)=(b, a+2b).

  • (0,3)(0, 3)(0,3): b=0b = 0b=0, a=3a = 3a=3, so [T(v1)]B=(3,0)[T(v_1)]_{\mathcal B} = (3, 0)[T(v1​)]B​=(3,0);
  • (2,6)(2, 6)(2,6): b=2b = 2b=2, a+4=6a + 4 = 6a+4=6 that is a=2a = 2a=2, so [T(v2)]B=(2,2)[T(v_2)]_{\mathcal B} = (2, 2)[T(v2​)]B​=(2,2).

Step 3: [T]BB=(3202)[T]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal B} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}[T]BB​=(30​22​). Among the answers there were also (2003)\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}(20​03​) (the matrix in the standard basis) and (0112)\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}(01​12​) (the basis vectors): they are the two classic traps.

Matters in the exam · Exam of 05/02/2026, question 6

Given T(x,y)=(3x, x+2y)T(x, y) = (3x,\ x + 2y)T(x,y)=(3x, x+2y) and the basis B={v1=(0,1), v2=(1,1)}\mathcal B = \{v_1 = (0, 1),\ v_2 = (1, 1)\}B={v1​=(0,1), v2​=(1,1)}, the coordinate vector [T(v1)]B[T(v_1)]_{\mathcal B}[T(v1​)]B​ is …

Solution. T(v1)=T(0,1)=(0,2)T(v_1) = T(0, 1) = (0, 2)T(v1​)=T(0,1)=(0,2). We look for a,ba, ba,b with a(0,1)+b(1,1)=(b, a+b)=(0,2)a (0, 1) + b (1, 1) = (b,\ a + b) = (0, 2)a(0,1)+b(1,1)=(b, a+b)=(0,2): b=0b = 0b=0 and a=2a = 2a=2. So [T(v1)]B=(2,0)[T(v_1)]_{\mathcal B} = (2, 0)[T(v1​)]B​=(2,0). The most tempting wrong answer was (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2), that is T(v1)T(v_1)T(v1​) itself: but the question asks for the coordinates.

Matters in the exam · Exam of 02/09/2025, question 5

Let f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W be linear with dim⁡V=4\dim V = 4dimV=4 and dim⁡W=2\dim W = 2dimW=2. Which is necessarily true?

Solution. By the rank–nullity theorem dim⁡Ker⁡f=4−dim⁡Im⁡f≥4−2=2\dim \Ker f = 4 - \dim \Imm f \ge 4 - 2 = 2dimKerf=4−dimImf≥4−2=2, so the kernel is never {0}\{0\}{0}: fff cannot be injective (it is point 1 of Proposition 15.3 read backwards). The other answers ("it must be surjective", "it cannot be surjective", "it must be injective", "it is an isomorphism") are false: the zero map is not surjective, while (x1,x2,x3,x4)↦(x1,x2)(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) \mapsto (x_1, x_2)(x1​,x2​,x3​,x4​)↦(x1​,x2​) is.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Writing the images in a row instead of in a column (you get the transpose).
  • Putting f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​) in the column instead of its coordinates with respect to the target basis.
  • Confusing the size: [f]CB[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[f]CB​ has dim⁡W\dim WdimW rows and dim⁡V\dim VdimV columns.
  • Changing the order of the basis vectors: the order of the columns follows the order of B\mathcal BB, the order of the rows follows that of C\mathcal CC.
  • For polynomials, forgetting that the coordinates with respect to {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2} are the coefficients from the constant term upwards.

Matters in the exam · The 4-page sheet

From this lesson three lines are enough: "column jjj of [f]CB[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[f]CB​ = [f(vj)]C[f(v_j)]_{\mathcal C}[f(vj​)]C​ (start at the top, target at the bottom)"; "[f(v)]C=[f]CB[v]B[f(v)]_{\mathcal C} = [f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} [v]_{\mathcal B}[f(v)]C​=[f]CB​[v]B​"; "fff injective ⇒dim⁡V≤dim⁡W\Rightarrow \dim V \le \dim W⇒dimV≤dimW, surjective ⇒dim⁡V≥dim⁡W\Rightarrow \dim V \ge \dim W⇒dimV≥dimW, isomorphic   ⟺  \iff⟺ same dimension".

1 · Exercise 15.13 of the handouts: a matrix with non-standard bases over C\CC intermediate

Consider the linear map

f:C2⟶C3,f(xy)=(x−y2xy).f : \C^2 \longrightarrow \C^3, \qquad f\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x - y \\ 2x \\ y \end{pmatrix}.f:C2⟶C3,f(xy​)=​x−y2xy​​.

Find the matrix associated with fff with respect to the bases v1=(1,1)v_1 = (1, 1)v1​=(1,1), v2=(1,−1)v_2 = (1, -1)v2​=(1,−1) at the start and w1=(1,1,0)w_1 = (1, 1, 0)w1​=(1,1,0), w2=(0,1,1)w_2 = (0, 1, 1)w2​=(0,1,1), w3=(1,0,1)w_3 = (1, 0, 1)w3​=(1,0,1) at the end.

Solution

The field is C\CC, but all the numbers involved are real: the calculations are the usual ones.

Step 1, the images:

f(v1)=f(1,1)=(1−1, 2, 1)=(0,2,1),f(v2)=f(1,−1)=(1+1, 2, −1)=(2,2,−1).f(v_1) = f(1, 1) = (1 - 1,\ 2,\ 1) = (0, 2, 1), \qquad f(v_2) = f(1, -1) = (1 + 1,\ 2,\ -1) = (2, 2, -1).f(v1​)=f(1,1)=(1−1, 2, 1)=(0,2,1),f(v2​)=f(1,−1)=(1+1, 2, −1)=(2,2,−1).

Step 2, coordinates with respect to w1,w2,w3w_1, w_2, w_3w1​,w2​,w3​. We write aw1+bw2+cw3=(a+c, a+b, b+c)a w_1 + b w_2 + c w_3 = (a + c,\ a + b,\ b + c)aw1​+bw2​+cw3​=(a+c, a+b, b+c).

For f(v1)=(0,2,1)f(v_1) = (0, 2, 1)f(v1​)=(0,2,1):

{a+c=0a+b=2b+c=1\begin{cases} a + c = 0 \\ a + b = 2 \\ b + c = 1 \end{cases}⎩⎨⎧​a+c=0a+b=2b+c=1​

From the first c=−ac = -ac=−a; the third becomes b−a=1b - a = 1b−a=1. Adding it to the second: 2b=32b = 32b=3, so b=32b = \frac 32b=23​; then a=2−32=12a = 2 - \frac 32 = \frac 12a=2−23​=21​ and c=−12c = -\frac 12c=−21​. So [f(v1)]C=(12,32,−12)[f(v_1)]_{\mathcal C} = \left(\frac 12, \frac 32, -\frac 12\right)[f(v1​)]C​=(21​,23​,−21​).

For f(v2)=(2,2,−1)f(v_2) = (2, 2, -1)f(v2​)=(2,2,−1):

{a+c=2a+b=2b+c=−1\begin{cases} a + c = 2 \\ a + b = 2 \\ b + c = -1 \end{cases}⎩⎨⎧​a+c=2a+b=2b+c=−1​

Subtracting the second from the first: c−b=0c - b = 0c−b=0, that is b=cb = cb=c. The third gives 2c=−12c = -12c=−1, so b=c=−12b = c = -\frac 12b=c=−21​ and a=2−c=52a = 2 - c = \frac 52a=2−c=25​. So [f(v2)]C=(52,−12,−12)[f(v_2)]_{\mathcal C} = \left(\frac 52, -\frac 12, -\frac 12\right)[f(v2​)]C​=(25​,−21​,−21​).

Step 3, the columns:

[f]CB=(1/25/23/2−1/2−1/2−1/2)=12(153−1−1−1).[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 5/2 \\ 3/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & -1/2 \end{pmatrix} = \frac 12 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}.[f]CB​=​1/23/2−1/2​5/2−1/2−1/2​​=21​​13−1​5−1−1​​.

It is the result given in the handouts. Check on the first column: 12(1,1,0)+32(0,1,1)−12(1,0,1)=(12−12, 12+32, 32−12)=(0,2,1)\frac 12 (1, 1, 0) + \frac 32 (0, 1, 1) - \frac 12 (1, 0, 1) = \left(\frac 12 - \frac 12,\ \frac 12 + \frac 32,\ \frac 32 - \frac 12\right) = (0, 2, 1)21​(1,1,0)+23​(0,1,1)−21​(1,0,1)=(21​−21​, 21​+23​, 23​−21​)=(0,2,1).

In lesson L16 you will find the same result again with the change-of-basis formula.

2 · Isomorphism or not? basic

For each linear map say whether it is an isomorphism, giving reasons: (a) f:R2→R2f : \R^2 \to \R^2f:R2→R2, f(x,y)=(x+y, x−y)f(x, y) = (x + y,\ x - y)f(x,y)=(x+y, x−y); (b) g:R3→R2g : \R^3 \to \R^2g:R3→R2, g(x,y,z)=(x,y)g(x, y, z) = (x, y)g(x,y,z)=(x,y); (c) h:R2[x]→R3h : \R_2[x] \to \R^3h:R2​[x]→R3, h(p)=(p(0),p(1),p(2))h(p) = (p(0), p(1), p(2))h(p)=(p(0),p(1),p(2)); (d) k:M(2,R)→M(2,R)k : M(2, \R) \to M(2, \R)k:M(2,R)→M(2,R), k(A)=A−tAk(A) = A - {}^tAk(A)=A−tA.

Solution

(a) Yes. Kernel: x+y=0x + y = 0x+y=0 and x−y=0x - y = 0x−y=0; adding, 2x=02x = 02x=0, so x=0x = 0x=0 and y=0y = 0y=0. Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0}, so fff is injective; since start and target have the same dimension 2, by the rank–nullity theorem dim⁡Im⁡f=2\dim \Imm f = 2dimImf=2 and fff is also surjective. (Alternatively: det⁡(111−1)=−2≠0\det \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = -2 \neq 0det(11​1−1​)=−2=0.)

(b) No. dim⁡R3=3≠2=dim⁡R2\dim \R^3 = 3 \neq 2 = \dim \R^2dimR3=3=2=dimR2: by Proposition 15.3 an isomorphism requires equal dimensions. Concretely g(0,0,1)=(0,0)g(0, 0, 1) = (0, 0)g(0,0,1)=(0,0), so ggg is not injective.

(c) Yes. With the basis {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2} at the start and the standard one at the end: h(1)=(1,1,1)h(1) = (1, 1, 1)h(1)=(1,1,1), h(x)=(0,1,2)h(x) = (0, 1, 2)h(x)=(0,1,2), h(x2)=(0,1,4)h(x^2) = (0, 1, 4)h(x2)=(0,1,4), so

[h]=(100111124),det⁡[h]=1⋅(1⋅4−1⋅2)=2≠0[h] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det [h] = 1 \cdot (1 \cdot 4 - 1 \cdot 2) = 2 \neq 0[h]=​111​012​014​​,det[h]=1⋅(1⋅4−1⋅2)=2=0

(expansion along the first row). The rank is 3, so Ker⁡h={0}\Ker h = \{0\}Kerh={0} and Im⁡h=R3\Imm h = \R^3Imh=R3. In words: a polynomial of degree at most 2 is determined by its values at three points.

(d) No. If A=(abcd)A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}A=(ac​bd​), then k(A)=(0b−cc−b0)k(A) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & b - c \\ c - b & 0 \end{pmatrix}k(A)=(0c−b​b−c0​). All the symmetric matrices (b=cb = cb=c) end up in 0, for example k(I2)=0k(I_2) = 0k(I2​)=0. The kernel is not {0}\{0\}{0} (it has dimension 3), so kkk is not injective.

3 · Coordinates in non-standard bases basic

(a) Find the coordinates of v=(5,1)v = (5, 1)v=(5,1) with respect to B={(1,1),(1,−1)}\mathcal B = \{(1, 1), (1, -1)\}B={(1,1),(1,−1)}. (b) Find the coordinates of p(x)=2x2−x+3p(x) = 2x^2 - x + 3p(x)=2x2−x+3 with respect to {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2} and with respect to B′={1, x−1, (x−1)2}\mathcal B' = \{1,\ x - 1,\ (x - 1)^2\}B′={1, x−1, (x−1)2}.

Solution

(a) λ1(1,1)+λ2(1,−1)=(5,1)\lambda_1 (1, 1) + \lambda_2 (1, -1) = (5, 1)λ1​(1,1)+λ2​(1,−1)=(5,1) gives λ1+λ2=5\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 5λ1​+λ2​=5 and λ1−λ2=1\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 1λ1​−λ2​=1. Adding: 2λ1=62\lambda_1 = 62λ1​=6, λ1=3\lambda_1 = 3λ1​=3; then λ2=2\lambda_2 = 2λ2​=2. So [v]B=(3,2)[v]_{\mathcal B} = (3, 2)[v]B​=(3,2). Check: 3(1,1)+2(1,−1)=(5,1)3(1, 1) + 2(1, -1) = (5, 1)3(1,1)+2(1,−1)=(5,1).

(b) With respect to {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2} the coefficients from the constant term upwards are enough: (3,−1,2)(3, -1, 2)(3,−1,2).

With respect to B′\mathcal B'B′ we look for a,b,ca, b, ca,b,c with

9 · Injective if and only if surjective hard

Let f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W be linear with dim⁡V=dim⁡W=n\dim V = \dim W = ndimV=dimW=n. Prove that fff is injective if and only if it is surjective. Then show with an example that the hypothesis dim⁡V=dim⁡W\dim V = \dim WdimV=dimW cannot be dropped.

Solution

By the rank–nullity theorem, n=dim⁡Ker⁡f+dim⁡Im⁡fn = \dim \Ker f + \dim \Imm fn=dimKerf+dimImf.

(⇒\Rightarrow⇒) If fff is injective, Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0}, so dim⁡Im⁡f=n=dim⁡W\dim \Imm f = n = \dim WdimImf=n=dimW. A subspace of WWW with the same dimension as WWW is the whole of WWW: a basis of it is made of nnn independent vectors of WWW, which by Theorem 7.12 are a basis of WWW. So Im⁡f=W\Imm f = WImf=W: fff is surjective.

(⇐\Leftarrow⇐) If fff is surjective, dim⁡Im⁡f=dim⁡W=n\dim \Imm f = \dim W = ndimImf=dimW=n, so dim⁡Ker⁡f=n−n=0\dim \Ker f = n - n = 0dimKerf=n−n=0, that is Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0}: fff is injective.

Without the hypothesis: g:R2→R3g : \R^2 \to \R^3g:R2→R3, g(x,y)=(x,y,0)g(x, y) = (x, y, 0)g(x,y)=(x,y,0) is injective but not surjective; h:R3→R2h : \R^3 \to \R^2h:R3→R2, h(x,y,z)=(x,y)h(x, y, z) = (x, y)h(x,y,z)=(x,y) is surjective but not injective.

§10

Review questions

self-check

Answer out loud or in writing, then open the answer.

What is an isomorphism? When are two spaces called isomorphic?

A bijective linear map, that is injective (Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0}) and surjective (Im⁡f=W\Imm f = WImf=W). Two spaces over the same field are isomorphic if there is at least one isomorphism between them.

Is the inverse of an isomorphism linear? Why?

Yes (Proposition 15.2). If f(v)=wf(v) = wf(v)=w and f(v′)=w′f(v') = w'f(v′)=w′, then f(v+v′)=w+w′f(v + v') = w + w'f(v+v′)=w+w′ and f(λv)=λwf(\lambda v) = \lambda wf(λv)=λw; since fff is bijective, this says that f−1(w+w′)=v+v′f^{-1}(w + w') = v + v'f−1(w+w′)=v+v′ and f−1(λw)=λvf^{-1}(\lambda w) = \lambda vf−1(λw)=λv.

What can you deduce about the dimensions if f:V→Wf : V \to Wf:V→W is injective? And if it is surjective?

Injective: dim⁡V=dim⁡Im⁡f≤dim⁡W\dim V = \dim \Imm f \le \dim WdimV=dimImf≤dimW. Surjective: dim⁡V≥dim⁡Im⁡f=dim⁡W\dim V \ge \dim \Imm f = \dim WdimV≥dimImf=dimW. Isomorphism: dim⁡V=dim⁡W\dim V = \dim WdimV=dimW. Everything comes from the rank–nullity theorem.

When are two finite-dimensional vector spaces isomorphic?

If and only if they have the same dimension (Proposition 15.4). In particular every space of dimension nnn over K\KK is isomorphic to Kn\K^nKn.

Which isomorphism V→KnV \to \K^nV→Kn do the handouts point to, and what does it depend on?

The map that sends every vector to its coordinates with respect to a basis of VVV. It depends on the basis: with different bases the same vector has different coordinates (for example x2x^2x2 is (0,0,1)(0, 0, 1)(0,0,1) in {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2} and (1,2,1)(1, 2, 1)(1,2,1) in {1,x−1,(x−1)2}\{1, x - 1, (x - 1)^2\}{1,x−1,(x−1)2}).

What does the associated matrix [f]CB[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[f]CB​ look like?

It is an m×nm \times nm×n matrix with m=dim⁡Wm = \dim Wm=dimW and n=dim⁡Vn = \dim Vn=dimV; column jjj contains the coordinates of f(vj)f(v_j)f(vj​) with respect to C\mathcal CC. The starting basis goes at the top, the target one at the bottom.

What is the matrix associated with LAL_ALA​ with respect to the standard bases?

It is AAA itself (Example 15.6): LA(ej)L_A(e_j)LA​(ej​) is column jjj of AAA, and its coordinates with respect to the standard basis are its components.

How do you compute f(v)f(v)f(v) using the associated matrix?

You write vvv in coordinates, [v]B[v]_{\mathcal B}[v]B​; you multiply: [f(v)]C=[f]CB[v]B[f(v)]_{\mathcal C} = [f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[v]_{\mathcal B}[f(v)]C​=[f]CB​[v]B​; finally, if C\mathcal CC is not the standard basis, you rebuild f(v)f(v)f(v) as a combination of the vectors of C\mathcal CC with those coefficients.

Why does the same map have different matrices?

Because the matrix records the coordinates of the images, and the coordinates depend on the bases chosen at the start and at the end (Examples 15.7 and 15.8).

What is [id⁡]BB[\id]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal B}[id]BB​? And [id⁡]CB[\id]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[id]CB​ with B≠C\mathcal B \neq \mathcal CB=C?

[id⁡]BB=In[\id]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal B} = I_n[id]BB​=In​ for every basis B\mathcal BB (Proposition 15.11). With two different bases it is generally not InI_nIn​: its columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B\mathcal BB with respect to C\mathcal CC (it is the change-of-basis matrix of lesson L16).

How do you add two linear maps, and what happens to the matrices?

(f+g)(v)=f(v)+g(v)(f + g)(v) = f(v) + g(v)(f+g)(v)=f(v)+g(v) and (λf)(v)=λf(v)(\lambda f)(v) = \lambda f(v)(λf)(v)=λf(v). Once the bases are fixed, [f+g]=[f]+[g][f + g] = [f] + [g][f+g]=[f]+[g] and [λf]=λ[f][\lambda f] = \lambda [f][λf]=λ[f].

What does Theorem 15.12 say?

That the linear maps V→WV \to WV→W form a vector space and that, once the bases are fixed, f↦[f]BAf \mapsto [f]^{\mathcal A}_{\mathcal B}f↦[f]BA​ is an isomorphism with M(m,n,K)M(m, n, \K)M(m,n,K): every m×nm \times nm×n matrix is the matrix of one and only one linear map.

§11

Glossary

terms
Injective
Different vectors have different images; for a linear map it is equivalent to Ker⁡f={0}\Ker f = \{0\}Kerf={0}.
Surjective
Every vector of the target space is the image of something: Im⁡f=W\Imm f = WImf=W.
Bijective
Injective and surjective; then the inverse f−1f^{-1}f−1 exists.
Isomorphism
Bijective linear map (Definition 15.1); its inverse is linear.
Isomorphic spaces
Spaces over the same field between which there is an isomorphism; in finite dimension, spaces with the same dimension.
Coordinates [v]B[v]_{\mathcal B}[v]B​
The column of the coefficients that write vvv as a combination of the vectors of the basis B\mathcal BB, in the order of the basis.
Ordered basis
A basis used as a list: the order of the vectors decides the order of the coordinates and of the columns.
Associated matrix [f]CB[f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}[f]CB​
m×nm \times nm×n matrix whose column jjj is [f(vj)]C[f(v_j)]_{\mathcal C}[f(vj​)]C​ (Definition 15.5).
Starting / target basis
The basis of the domain (at the top in the notation) and that of the codomain (at the bottom).
LAL_ALA​
The map x↦Axx \mapsto Axx↦Ax; its matrix in the standard bases is AAA.
Coordinate formula
[f(v)]C=[f]CB [v]B[f(v)]_{\mathcal C} = [f]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal C}\,[v]_{\mathcal B}[f(v)]C​=[f]CB​[v]B​ (Proposition 15.9).
Matrix of the identity
[id⁡]BB=In[\id]^{\mathcal B}_{\mathcal B} = I_n[id]BB​=In​ for every basis B\mathcal BB (Proposition 15.11).
Sum of maps
(f+g)(v)=f(v)+g(v)(f + g)(v) = f(v) + g(v)(f+g)(v)=f(v)+g(v); the matrix of the sum is the sum of the matrices.
Hom(V,W)\mathrm{Hom}(V, W)Hom(V,W)
Name used in Martelli's book for the space of linear maps V→WV \to WV→W; it has dimension dim⁡V⋅dim⁡W\dim V \cdot \dim WdimV⋅dimW.
Rank–nullity theorem
dim⁡V=dim⁡Ker⁡f+dim⁡Im⁡f\dim V = \dim \Ker f + \dim \Imm fdimV=dimKerf+dimImf (lesson L14): it is the basis of all the properties about dimensions.
